# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1–29 (Complete – Updated 2026-10-13)

## Setting and Time
- **Current Period**: Spring of eighth year after Waterloo, continuing into summer and beyond. Year is 1830 (French Revolution year). John Sedley deceased (died peacefully, buried at Brompton). Mr. Osborne deceased (four days after stroke). Major Dobbin appointed executor. Rawdon governs Coventry Island. Georgy established as heir.
- **Locations**: London (multiple districts); Coventry Island; Queen's Crawley; Coldcombe and Mirecombe farms; Bryngate (market town); Pumpernickel (German principality); Ostend (seaside resort); Hampshire (Dobbin's rented country place "the Evergreens," near Queen's Crawley); Brussels; Aix-la-Chapelle; Bath and Cheltenham; Welbeck Street, London.

## Rebecca's Seduction and Integration (Chapters 27–28)
**Encounter and Manipulation**: At Pumpernickel Stadthaus gaming, Rebecca (Madame de Raudon, formerly with Rawdon Crawley) encountered Jos Sedley. Led him to Room No. 92, Elephant lodging-house. Through calculated seduction—hiding degradation evidence, offering tender looks, claiming heart first beat at his presence—convinced Jos she was virtuous and wronged. Revealed true nature to Max and Fritz (Schoppenhausen students): bohemian, boastful. Had falsely advertised Leipzig concert; won money at trente-et-quarante using young Georgy.

**Dobbin's Opposition**: Dobbin called her "the little minx," mistrusted her, recalled Rawdon was "confounded blackleg." Jos resented Dobbin's superiority; stormy colloquy followed. Becky arrived with meagre baggage; Amelia embraced her warmly, flung Dobbin "an angry look—the most unjust and scornful glance" of her life. **FACT: Dobbin had spent fifteen years devoted to Amelia; she had grown accustomed to trampling on him but did not wish to marry him—only to keep him.** Dobbin departed with haughty bow.

**False Narrative and Household Integration**: Becky claimed child "torn from her arms shrieking" by Rawdon's cruelty; bore poverty and neglect; driven to demand separation when Rawdon asked her sacrifice fair fame for Marquis of Steyne advancement. Within week, Jos became "sworn slave and frantic admirer." Becky discovered how to soothe Emmy: praised Dobbin constantly, told her she had behaved cruelly toward him, made Georgy write constantly to Major. Changed habits—no more torn collars, rouge-pot suspended, spirit-and-water indulged only privately.

**Jos's Miniature and Amelia's Regret**: Boxes from Leipzig arrived. Becky took gentleman's miniature in pencil (Jos's), face painted pink, riding on elephant. Jos delighted; Emmy tired and unwell. Amelia made aware of Dobbin's movements through Georgy's correspondence. William wrote "in a manner so unconstrainedly cold" that Amelia "felt now in her turn that she had lost her power over him." He was free. "He had left her, and she was wretched."

**Dobbin's Career and Summer Revelations**: Dobbin joined --th regiment at Chatham. Promoted to Lieutenant-Colonel; Colonel Sir Michael O'Dowd advanced to Major-General with indication Dobbin should become Colonel of distinguished regiment. During summer evenings, Emmy told Georgy that William was "best man in all the world"; reminded Georgy he owed everything to Dobbin's benevolent care.

**Dobbin's Final Speech and Rejection**: William told Amelia: "I have loved you and watched you for fifteen years in vain...You are not worthy of the love which I have devoted to you...I will bargain no more: I withdraw...Good-bye, Amelia!" He broke the chain by which she held him, left with "head on his breast"; never looked back. Georgy burst out crying. Emmy cleared away Dobbin's books and stored them with her work-box.

## Chapter 29 – Ostend Crisis, George's Infidelity Revealed, and Dobbin's Reconciliation
**Disreputable Company at Ostend**: Doctor von Glauber convinced Jos that both he and Emmy needed summer at Ostend. Becky came "as a matter of course" in Jos's fine barouche. At Ostend, scores of Becky's acquaintances cut her; Amelia, who "knew nobody, was not aware of the treatment." Major Loder (unattached) and Captain Rook (late of the Rifles) invaded dinner-table, made "advances that filled her with sickening dismay." **"A couple of ruffians were fighting for this innocent creature, gambling for her at her own table."** Amelia sent secret letter "to a friend whom she had on the other side of the water."

**Becky's Revelation of George's Infidelity**: Becky revealed George Osborne was "that selfish humbug, that low-bred cockney dandy...who had neither wit, nor manners, nor heart." **"The man was weary of you, and would have jilted you, but that Dobbin forced him to keep his word. He owned it to me...He made love to me the week after he married you."** Becky produced letter: George "wanted me to run away with him—gave it me under your nose, the day before he was shot—and served him right!"

**Amelia's Transformation**: Emmy's head sank; "for almost the last time in which she shall be called upon to weep in this history, she commenced that work." Internal analysis: "Was she most grieved because the idol of her life was tumbled down...or glad because the barrier was removed which modesty had placed between her and a new, a real affection? 'There is nothing to forbid me now,' she thought. 'I may love him with all my heart now.'"

**Dobbin's Arrival and Reconciliation**: Two mornings later, Amelia insisted on walking Dike with Georgy. English steamer appeared; Georgy spotted through telescope: "There's a man lying down, and a—chap in a—cloak—Hooray!—it's Dob, by Jingo!" As gentleman in old cloak stepped ashore, "A lady in a dripping white bonnet and shawl, with her two little hands out before her, went up to him...she had altogether disappeared under the folds of the old cloak, and was kissing one of his hands with all her might."

**Marriage and New Life**: Only Georgy and Jos present at marriage ceremony. Emmy told William: "Never speak of that day again," asking his account of Glorvina and Peggy O'Dowd instead. Becky, "satisfied with her part in the transaction," claimed "particular business" took her to Bruges; never presented herself before Colonel Dobbin and his bride. Glorvina married Major Posky after his first wife's death. Lady O'Dowd lives in "great splendour at O'Dowdstown" with Colonel Sir Michael (now Major-General). Colonel Dobbin quit service immediately after marriage, rented "the Evergreens" (Hampshire country place, near Queen's Crawley). Lady Jane and Mrs. Dobbin became great friends. Lady Jane godmother to Mrs. Dobbin's child (christened Jane, by Rev. James Crawley). George and Rawdon (Sir Pitt's son) hunted and shot together, entered same college at Cambridge, quarrelled over Lady Jane's daughter.

## Jos Sedley's Decline and Death
**Insurance and Dobbin's Investigation**: Rebecca remained Jos's constant companion on continent, "entirely her slave." Colonel's lawyers informed Dobbin that Jos had effected heavy insurance upon his life, probable he had been raising money to discharge debts. He procured prolonged leave of absence from East India House; his infirmities were daily increasing.

**Brussels Meeting**: Dobbin, alarmed, went to Brussels where Jos then was, living in enormous hotel. Mrs. Crawley occupied another suite of apartments in same hotel, had her carriage, gave entertainments, lived in very genteel manner. Jos begged Dobbin to visit when Mrs. Crawley would be at soiree; they could meet alone. Dobbin found Jos in "condition of pitiable infirmity--and dreadfully afraid of Rebecca, though eager in his praises of her. She tended him through a series of unheard-of illnesses with a fidelity most admirable. She had been a daughter to him." Jos pleaded: "but--but--oh, for God's sake, do come and live near me, and--and--see me sometimes."

**Death and Will**: Dobbin never saw Jos more. Three months afterwards Joseph Sedley died at Aix-la-Chapelle. All his property had been "muddled away in speculations, and was represented by valueless shares in different bubble companies." All available assets were the two thousand pounds for which his life was insured, left equally between his beloved "sister Amelia, wife of, &c., and his friend and invaluable attendant during sickness, Rebecca, wife of Lieutenant-Colonel Rawdon Crawley, C.B.," who was appointed administratrix.

## Insurance Dispute and Rebecca's Victory
**Company's Challenge**: Solicitor of insurance company swore it was "the blackest case that ever had come before him," talked of sending commission to Aix to examine into death; Company refused payment. Rebecca came to town at once (attended with solicitors, Messrs. Burke, Thurtell, and Hayes, of Thavies Inn) and dared Company to refuse payment. They invited examination, declared she was object of "infamous conspiracy, which had been pursuing her all through life," and triumphed finally. Money was paid, character established. **Colonel Dobbin sent back his share of legacy to insurance office and rigidly declined to hold any communication with Rebecca.**

## Rawdon Crawley's Death and Estate Succession
**Colonel Rawdon's Death**: His Excellency Colonel Rawdon Crawley died of yellow fever at Coventry Island, "most deeply beloved and deplored," and six weeks before demise of his brother, Sir Pitt. Estate consequently devolved upon present Sir Rawdon Crawley, Bart. (Sir Pitt's son).

**The Young Baronet and Rebecca**: Sir Rawdon lives entirely at Queen's Crawley with Lady Jane and her daughter. He has declined to see his mother (Rebecca), to whom he makes liberal allowance; she appears very wealthy. Rebecca, who never became Lady Crawley though continues so to call herself, chiefly hangs about Bath and Cheltenham, where strong party of excellent people consider her "a most injured woman."

## Rebecca's Final State
**Respectability and Charitable Work**: Rebecca busies herself in works of piety. Goes to church never without footman. Name in all Charity Lists. Destitute orange-girl, neglected washerwoman, distressed muffin-man find in her "a fast and generous friend." Always having stalls at Fancy Fairs for benefit of hapless beings. **Emmy, her children, and Colonel Dobbin encountered her at one of these fairs; she cast down her eyes demurely and smiled as they started away; Emmy scurried off on arm of George (now grown dashing young gentleman) and Colonel seized up his little Janey, of whom he is fonder than anything in world--fonder even than of his History of the Punjaub.**

## Final Character States
- **Amelia & William**: Married, reconciled; barrier to true love removed; William achieved his objective of fifteen years; child Jane christened; he is devoted father and historian.
- **Rebecca**: Architect of revelation and Jos's death; never became Lady Crawley but styles herself so; wealthy; living in Bath/Cheltenham; performs charitable works; has enemies; her life is her answer.
- **Jos**: Deceased at Aix-la-Chapelle; enslaved to Becky until death; left fortune split between Amelia and Rebecca.
- **Georgy (now George)**: Son of Amelia and William; grown dashing young gentleman; befriended Rawdon; entered same college as Rawdon.
- **Sir Rawdon Crawley, Bart.**: Young baronet; inherits after father's death at Coventry Island; lives at Queen's Crawley with Lady Jane; declined to see mother Rebecca.
